ordered.note: Tick what is requested and number it: 1 is the most preferred, and an authenticator uses the first it supports. A number on an unticked row is ignored; two rows with the same number keep the order they are drawn in.
section.applies: Applies to the next token, assertion, ticket or search — nothing already issued changes.
section.readAtStartup: Every setting in this section is read at startup, so there is nothing here to save. Change them in {file} or in the environment and restart.
shared.rest: One setting, shown in both places because it governs both: a value saved here is saved there. Nothing is copied — both forms post to the same action against the same override map.
forms.heading: Settings
forms.lead1: The appconfig rows that decide what this family does, on the page for the family rather than on
forms.lead2: . They are the same settings, written through the same function against the same override map — this is a second DOOR onto them and not a second place they live, which is the rule
forms.lead3: was the first page here to apply. The Source column says where each value came from: a runtime override set on a page like this one, an environment variable, the appconfig file this process was started with, or the default appconfig file under it.
forms.kept: Changes here SURVIVE A RESTART. This process is running with persistence.mode={mode}, so a value set here is written to the persistent store and applied again the next time this service starts. It is still a runtime override rather than a new layer — the same setting, the same override map, put back through the same function — so Reset still means "fall back to the file or the environment variable", and the reset is written down too. Nothing rewrites {file}, deliberately: a service that edited a file checked into a repository would leave a test's forgotten change behind permanently. See
forms.keptRealm: Changes here SURVIVE A RESTART. This process is running with persistence.mode={mode}, so a value set here is written to the persistent store with the {realm} realm's row and applied again the next time this service starts. It is still a runtime override rather than a new layer — the same setting, the same override map, put back through the same function — so Reset still means "fall back to the file or the environment variable", and the reset is written down too. Nothing rewrites {file}, deliberately: a service that edited a file checked into a repository would leave a test's forgotten change behind permanently. See
forms.memory: Changes here are in memory and are gone on restart. Nothing writes to the appconfig file, deliberately: a service that edited a file checked into a repository would leave a test's forgotten change behind permanently. To make something stick, put it in {file}, in the setting's environment variable, or turn on a persistent store — see
forms.memoryRealm: Changes here are in memory and are gone on restart. Nothing writes to the appconfig file, deliberately: a service that edited a file checked into a repository would leave a test's forgotten change behind permanently. To make something stick, put it in {file}, in the setting's environment variable, or turn on a persistent store with persistence.realms, which keeps this realm's own values on its row — see
forms.fixed: {fixed} of these {all} cannot be changed while this service runs. They are shown with their inputs disabled and the reason beside each, rather than hidden: they were consumed by the time this service was listening — a bound socket, a certificate's names, the Kerberos principal database and its long-term keys, the directory's base DN — and accepting a change to one would do nothing and read as having worked.
